title: Psalm 64: Arrows of the Tongue, Arrows of God
summary: David asks God to hide him from a gang of schemers who sharpen their tongues like swords and shoot bitter words from ambush, confident that no one sees them. But God shoots back: suddenly they are wounded, their own tongues turn against them, and everyone who sees fears God. The righteous rejoice and take refuge in the LORD.
story: Psalm 64 closes the small group of Davidic trust psalms in 61 to 64 and is the last lament before the three great songs of praise in Psalms 65 to 67. Its concern is a particular kind of attack: not armies or physical violence but words, slander, and secret plotting. The earlier psalms in this stretch described enemies with sharp tongues (Psalm 57:4; 59:7), and this one makes that the whole subject. Its ending, in which all people see God's work and fear him, prepares for the next psalms, where all the earth is called to praise.
historical:
The heading names David and the choirmaster but no occasion. David's life offers many examples of the kind of attack described here: Saul's courtiers who spoke against him, Doeg the Edomite who informed on him and the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:9-10; Psalm 52), and the Ziphites who betrayed his hiding place (1 Samuel 23:19). Later, Absalom won the people's hearts with flattering words at the city gate before his rebellion (2 Samuel 15:1-6). Any of these could stand behind the psalm, but it doesn't name one, and it was clearly meant to be usable by anyone facing organized slander.

The psalm's concern with secret plots also reflects the world of ancient courts and cities, where reputation was essential to survival. An accusation spread by a group of people could lead to ruin, exile, or death, and the law of Moses took false witness seriously enough to punish the false witness with the penalty he intended for his victim (Deuteronomy 19:16-19).
cultural:
The psalm's central image is archery. In the ancient Near East the bow was a primary weapon of war and hunting, and an archer could shoot from cover without being seen. Verse 4 pictures the schemers “ambushing the innocent in seclusion, shooting suddenly, without fear,” firing words the way a hidden archer fires arrows. Their confidence rests on the belief that no one sees: “Who will see them?” they say. In a world where public accusation could destroy a person, secret speech was a real weapon.

The reaction of the onlookers in verse 8, who shake their heads, was a common gesture of scorn or astonishment at someone's downfall (Psalm 22:7; Jeremiah 18:16). When the schemers fall, the crowd that might once have believed them now mocks them.
literary: The psalm is built on a reversal. Verses 1 to 6 describe the wicked sharpening their tongues and shooting arrows suddenly from hiding. Verses 7 to 10 answer that God will shoot them with arrows and “suddenly they will be wounded.” The Hebrew repeats the same words, shoot and suddenly, so that the punishment matches the crime exactly. Verse 8 adds another twist: their own tongues are turned against them. The first half ends with a comment on the depths of the human heart (verse 6), and the second half ends with all people pondering God's work (verse 9). The psalm moves from secret plotting to public understanding, and from the fear the enemies cause to the fear of God that their fall produces.

outline.t: A plea for protection from secret schemers
Tongues like swords, words like arrows
Hidden snares and the depths of the heart
God shoots back, and their tongues turn on them
All people fear, and the righteous rejoice

doctrines.note: The psalm exposes the sins of the tongue: slander, bitter words, and secret plotting. It says the inner man and the heart are deep, hidden from human view, but not from God.
God's judgment matches the wrong done: those who shot arrows are shot, and their own tongues bring them down. Justice is not arbitrary but fitting.
The wicked believe no one sees them. The psalm answers that God sees and acts, and that his acts become public so that people learn from them.

words.note: Lashon, tongue. In verse 3 the wicked sharpen their tongues like swords, and in verse 8 their own tongues are turned against them. The tongue is a constant concern of the Psalms and Proverbs, which see speech as a weapon that can wound as deeply as a blade (Proverbs 12:18; James 3:5-8).
Pitom, suddenly. It appears in verse 4, where the wicked shoot suddenly, and in verse 7, where they are suddenly wounded. The repetition marks the reversal: the ambush they planned becomes their own.

Yarah, to shoot. The verb appears for the wicked shooting at the innocent and for God shooting at the wicked. Related forms of the root are used elsewhere for teaching or pointing the way, and the noun torah, instruction, is often connected to it, though the psalm uses the verb in its plain sense of shooting arrows.

Amoq, deep. Verse 6 says the inner man and the heart are deep. The line can be read as the enemies' boast that their plans are too deep to discover, or as the psalmist's comment on the hidden depths of human wickedness. Either way, what is deep to people is not hidden from God (Jeremiah 17:9-10).

christ: Jesus was the target of secret plots and false words: the leaders plotted to arrest him by stealth (Matthew 26:3-4), and false witnesses testified against him (Mark 14:55-59). Unlike the psalmist, he did not ask for his enemies to be struck down but entrusted himself to the Father who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). The resurrection reversed the verdict of those who plotted against him, much as the psalm describes God reversing the schemes of the wicked. James warns that the tongue is a fire (James 3:6), echoing the Psalms' concern with speech. The connections are thematic, but they show Jesus as the innocent one who suffered exactly the kind of attack this psalm describes.
questions: The psalm describes words as weapons. When have you been wounded by words, and when have your words wounded others?
The wicked say, “Who will see them?” How does knowing that God sees change the way you speak about others in private?
The psalm ends with the righteous taking refuge in the LORD. What does it look like to take refuge in God when you are being slandered or misunderstood?
